episodes.summary: Reacting to Channel 4's 'Can AI Steal Your Vote?', Matt and Jimmy dissect how a fake social app fed deepfakes of Sunak and Starmer to 25 voters and swayed 23 of them within two weeks — often with a single targeted fear like a £35 GP charge. They widen the lens to AI-cloned news anchors in India, a Kate Middleton imprisonment deepfake circulating on WeChat, and the collapse of trustable evidence, landing on practical defences: read manifestos, think critically, and get off social media before elections.
keyTalkingPoints: Channel 4 experiment: 23 of 25 voters swung by AI-generated content in two weeks via the fake 'Echo' app
One well-targeted sentence (NHS £35 charge, immigrants atop housing lists) was enough to flip most participants
India: cloned news-anchor deepfakes produced in hours, in multiple languages, all accepted and published on YouTube
China: a fake Kate Middleton 'imprisoned by William' video was allowed through censorship to brew as clickbait
Even after debunks, anger persists — the 'synapse is already rewired'; confirmation bias beats corrections
Defences: read party manifestos directly, critical thinking, avoid social media before elections, Ground News slider

jimmy: Even AI-aware viewers can be fooled by good deepfakes, and the unaware have no reason to doubt them
Mainstream media has so far debunked big deepfakes quickly, but lower-profile races and swing states are the real risk
The answer is critical thinking and questioning everything online — tiring, but the alternative is being sold a lie
For elections specifically, people should read manifestos and watch debates rather than trust clips
matt: Evidence itself is no longer believable — we are in a 'post post-truth' world staring at 99%-real fakes
He does not trust fact-checkers or mainstream media in general; only self-verification and manifestos
Companies and states will steer even innocent joke deepfakes once they go viral, as China's censors did
Admits he has been struggling for months to know what to believe and recommends steering clear of social media

predictions.claim: Deepfake efforts will concentrate on the November 2024 US election as the big target.
predictions.quote: the US election is the big one and I think getting this kind of stuff out there ahead of of, you know, November

predictions.claim: It is only a matter of time before a major AI disinformation operation gets past mainstream media scrutiny.
predictions.quote: what would be interesting for me is when, when is the first one of these going to get past the mainstream media, so to speak?

predictions.claim: As deepfakes get easier, low-profile races in smaller places will be nudged without media spotlight.
predictions.quote: what about in lower profile stuff that isn't in the media spotlight, where you know you could actually be nudging swing states in, like smaller rural places

episodes.summary: Self-described generalist Ben Cook argues AI is a bottom-up empowerment revolution: from ranking job candidates in minutes to building a call-center QA prototype with no software background. He pushes back on doom with Luddite history and washing-machine analogies, insisting new jobs will come and humans stay in the loop, while conceding there is an investment-driven bubble and that specialists face the greatest risk.
keyTalkingPoints: 'Age of the generalist': LLMs brief anyone on any field; specialists whose life work is a narrow task are most exposed
LLMs shine on repetitive flows needing a touch of creativity; tightly-guarded rails still wobble (prompt injection, 'eyeball soup')
Regulation: EU over-regulates, US regulates after the fact, China regulates the algorithm — Matt calls China's 'best of the bunch'
Hype cycle: at the top and driven by investment needs, but there will be '50 hype cycles'; short-term overestimated, long-term underestimated
Education: LLM-as-patient-teacher beats declaring 'code red'; teach logic and interpretation, not syntax
Matt predicts social unrest and data-center attacks once robots take manual jobs; Ben counters with no-mass-unemployment history

jimmy: Boxed, prescriptive LLM tasks (CV ranking, extraction) barely hallucinate — the use case Ben demos is one of the best
The hype faded because economic benefits are a slower burn; most people still treat chatbots as toys
Dismissive coders should get on board now — the models improve exponentially and burying your head in the sand is the worst option
LLMs are not calculators; judging them on maths misses what they are for
matt: Agrees AI empowers generalists but keeps his gaze existential and long-term — short-term hype, underestimated long-term risks
Quotes Keith Teare: Aschenbrenner overestimates short-term and underestimates long-term impacts; we are at the top of a hype cycle
China's algorithm-focused regulation is the best of the bunch; the UK is carving out a genuine safety/governance niche
Predicts some social unrest, attacks on data centers and a public backlash against figures like Sam Altman

predictions.claim: Within 5-10 years, job applicants will be expected to have AI skills, even if only chatbot use.
predictions.quote: There's going to be an expectation in 5, 10 years'time that when you are applying for a job, that you have skills in using AI, even if it's AI chatbots

predictions.claim: At some point people will attack data centers and figures like Sam Altman will struggle to appear in public.
predictions.quote: but that there will be at least some level of people that attack data centers and you know people like sam altman will find it difficult to go out in public because there'll be enough of a backlash.

predictions.claim: There is an AI bubble and the hype has already started to deflate.
predictions.quote: There is a bubble. There's definitely, I mean, the hype cycle. Has it started to deflate? Yet I feel like things have kind of gone off the boil a bit recently.

predictions.claim: Most podcasts will eventually be AI-generated, so human podcasters have limited time left.
predictions.quote: there is a school of thought that most podcasts will just be ai generated, so we probably haven't got that long left

episodes.summary: The first 'emergency episode' responds to Ilya Sutskever founding Safe Superintelligence days after their relaunch call-to-arms: Matt wants to believe Ilya but questions how safety-first wins an ASI race against investor pressure, quoting Zvi Moshkowitz's 'worst possible thing' critique. They also cover Claude 3.5 Sonnet topping benchmarks at a fifth of Opus's cost, the UK AISI's pre-release safety evaluation, and the Glasgow paper arguing ChatGPT is 'bullshit'.
keyTalkingPoints: SSI aims for a 'straight shot' to safe ASI — but you cannot reach ASI without passing AGI, and alignment of a superintelligence may be impossible
Matt believes Ilya is genuine but 'Sam Altman is now the devil'; trillion-dollar compute needs will let investors tip the balance
Zvi Moshkowitz quote: Ilya is 'the latest to do the worst possible thing', calling it 'safe' is not an improvement
Claude 3.5 Sonnet beats Opus and GPT-4o across benchmarks while faster and roughly five times cheaper; best-in-class vision
UK AISI ran a pre-release safety evaluation — Britain is 'walking the walk' on governance and pressures OpenAI to follow
Hicks et al (Glasgow): LLMs produce 'soft bullshit' (no concern for truth) and maybe 'hard bullshit' (designed to seem truth-seeking)

jimmy: Most curious how SSI could technically make a superintelligence safe — a truly superhuman system would have something like free will
If SSI succeeds it may force OpenAI to put safety back on the agenda; the announcement keeps safety in the headlines either way
Claude 3.5 Sonnet is the best model right now — Anthropic is superseding OpenAI in quality, speed and cost
The 'ChatGPT is bullshit' paper is welcome coping — LLMs are not as advanced as their makers claim
matt: Torn: believes Ilya's intentions but thinks investor pressure will eventually corrupt any safety-first ASI venture
The real positive is narrative — the industry's top technical mind putting safety first legitimizes the whole governance agenda
Anthropic has taken the ethical seat OpenAI vacated; SSI adds a player and decentralizes power in the race
Quotes Zvi's pessimistic take and demands substance: 'How is he going to make it safe? His statements tell us nothing'

predictions.claim: Claude 3.5 Sonnet will soon be followed by 3.5 versions of Opus and Haiku.
predictions.quote: It's going to be followed, I would imagine, by a version 3.5 of Opus and Haiku.

predictions.claim: Anthropic is ahead for now, but the model lead will probably change hands within weeks.
predictions.quote: at the moment they're ahead in the race, but you know it'll probably change in a few weeks time, I'm sure

predictions.claim: If SSI brings safety to the forefront it could force OpenAI to rethink and put safety back on the agenda.
predictions.quote: if it brings safety to the forefront, then maybe it forces companies like OpenAI to have a little bit of a rethink and to actually start putting safety on the agenda again.

predictions.claim: Soon someone will claim ASI is achievable imminently, as they already do for AGI.
predictions.quote: I think no one has kind of claimed that ASI is possible by September or 2024, where they have for AGI, although maybe that's going to change.

episodes.summary: The season-two relaunch is Matt's 'call to arms': with experts putting 20–99.999% odds on AI existential risk (Hinton 50-50 within 5–20 years), only two paths avoid dystopia — a catastrophic 'there goes Tokyo' incident or a mass public-sentiment shift forcing governments to regulate frontier-model development. They argue self-regulation is dead (OpenAI disbanded its safety team; Nadella: 'we are below them, above them, around them'), the EU AI Act governs use not development, and propose nuclear-style embedded inspectors while Jimmy explains alignment and universal jailbreaks.
keyTalkingPoints: P(doom): Hinton puts human vs advanced AI conflict at 50-50 within 5-20 years; Jampolsky ~99.999...%; 20% is the agreed 'floor'
Two ways out: a catastrophic AI incident sparking global backlash, or massive public sentiment shift — Matt thinks option two is already too late
AI unlike nuclear: no deterrent (a better AI can disarm yours) and under 10% of spend on safety versus ~90% for nuclear
EU AI Act is the gold standard but regulates use/application, not frontier model development where the existential risk lives
OpenAI coup aftermath: safety-minded board members all out; Microsoft is ubiquitous and gets a free pass; Nvidia is the fuel of the AI fire
Alignment primer: black-box training, RLHF, universal jailbreaks (Pliny has jailbroken every major model); future models will act, not just talk

jimmy: Three or four big tech firms self-govern for PR — self-regulation has never worked, so governments and people must act
Regulating AI resembles fighting tax loopholes: companies can outspend regulators, making it 'almost a non-starter' — but still worth pushing
Job losses will make AI a real political topic; governments regulate impacts, which is their comfort zone
AI creeping into power grids and industries is a huge slow danger — massive centralization of power in coming years
matt: Relaunch manifesto: dedicate every resource to safe development — 'there is no rule that says we'll make it' (Robert Miles)
Two ways to avoid dystopia and the sentiment-shift option is already too late, so the podcast must catalyze pressure
The EU Act does not touch model development, which is what must be governed; nuclear-style inspectorate embedded in labs is the model
Pause if you cannot prove safety; AI is one of the world's three big issues and could make the others irrelevant

predictions.claim: Once 2024's elections settle, AI governance will be higher on the political agenda.
predictions.quote: When the dust settles from those, I think this will be more on the agenda and I think there is a space to start making a difference and getting involved in that space.

predictions.claim: Rising visible job losses from AI are when it becomes a real topic of political discussion.
predictions.quote: As we start to see those, as we start to see more and more job losses and AI replacing jobs and robots replacing jobs and all the things we've talked about in previous episodes. I think that's when it will start to become a real topic for discussion

predictions.claim: Existential threats from AI could arrive in three years or thirty — nobody knows, so development must be governed now.
predictions.quote: they could be 20 years away, 30 years away or three years away. We just don't know

predictions.claim: AI enables a massive centralization of power and resources over the coming years.
predictions.quote: there's huge potential for a massive kind of centralization of power resource whatever you want to call it over the like coming years

episodes.summary: After a news catch-up — Apple's ChatGPT-in-Siri privacy paradox and Reuters/Oxford data showing only 1–7% daily AI use across six countries — the hosts soft-launch a relaunch toward governance and alignment. Guest Daniel Lyons explains PR adoption is still executional (monitoring, data analysis, translation; ~40% of tasks AI-assisted) and held back by skills gaps, billing ethics, and above all trust, while Matt calls prompt-engineering careers 'bollocks' and argues crisis-management AI is only a couple of years away.
keyTalkingPoints: Apple Intelligence integrating ChatGPT into Siri contradicts Apple's privacy brand; dedicated AI hardware like the Rabbit is stillborn
Reuters Institute: ~30% across six countries never heard of any AI tool; daily use 1% Japan, 2% UK/France; Claude awareness 2-5%
PR: AI does monitoring/data analysis/translation; strategic work (crisis, relationships) stays human — CIPR figure ~40% of tasks AI-assisted
Prompt engineers/architects: Matt — 'bollocks... an industry that might exist for a year and then it's gone' as models understand natural language
Trust is the No.1 adoption barrier — 'we never asked for this'; EU AI Act will force AI-content labeling; human-made quality marks may emerge
Future: 'boardroom AI advisor' in business-continuity plans; one-person AI agencies could out-compete big firms

jimmy: People already use AI daily without knowing it — integration into search and phones delivers ubiquity without awareness
Generative AI is a cheat around writer's block: scaffolding you rewrite; AI-assisted labeling of content will become unworkable
Expects the first billion-dollar one-person AI companies within 5-10 years, massively disrupting service industries
China's AI rules include progressive worker-protection measures — worth a dedicated regulation episode
matt: Awareness of AI tools matters less than awareness of AI's coming societal change — and most people have neither, which scares him
Trust in AI will never be fully overcome 'in our lifetimes' — it is the biggest barrier, and it is about who controls AI
Prompt-engineering as a career is 'for the birds'; AI crisis-management tools are maybe a couple of years off and will strip out teams
Credits named cuts over stealth cuts, but expects regulation to arrive too late for many people

predictions.claim: PR industry hesitancy about AI will fade within 6-12 months and structural impact will follow.
predictions.quote: but I think within the next sort of six months you know 12 months I think I think that will slowly sort of ever way and then actually the sort of the industry itself will sort of start to see the impact

predictions.claim: AI crisis-management systems capable of handling organizational nuance are only a couple of years off.
predictions.quote: I don't think it's a long way off, I think it's maybe a couple of years off, but you can easily see a model being created that allows you know within an organization for it to pick up the nuance, to be able to do most of that crisis management.

predictions.claim: Within 5-10 years the first one-person-plus-AI company worth billions will emerge.
predictions.quote: maybe in the next five, ten years, we'll see the first sort of you know company that's just one person and a bunch of ais, who becomes worth you know billions of dollars

predictions.claim: Within a year, far more people will be thinking about, worrying about and acting on AI.
predictions.quote: a lot more people will be thinking about and worrying about and acting on and you know, getting involved with AI. I'm pretty sure that's the case.

episodes.summary: The hosts argue the pace of AI job losses has stepped up: viral first-person accounts from a graphic designer (nade straight, ~750k views) and a copywriter (Ashen Guardian), plus hard corporate announcements — BT cutting ~40% of roles by 2028-2030 with 10,000 direct AI replacements, and IBM pausing non-customer-facing hiring (~7,800 roles). An anonymous publishing veteran describes senior editorial jobs replaced by junior 'social and AI' hires, Google AI answers gutting referral traffic, and generative content convergence, before Hinton's UBI plea and Musk's 'universal high income' close the episode.
keyTalkingPoints: Microsoft Copilot Plus PCs add an NPU plus 'Recall' snapshots of everything — useful but a privacy own goal; on-device LLMs are the positive
Anthropic's Golden Gate Claude: amplifying one feature gave the model an identity crisis — the first real look inside a frontier model
BT: 130k staff to 75-80k by 2028-30 (40%), including 10,000 roles as direct AI replacements; IBM: hiring freeze on ~7,800 back-office roles
Anonymous guest: it is senior jobs going, replaced by juniors with 'social and AI experience'; Google AI overviews slash referral traffic
If trained writers cannot earn, models run out of lived-experience data; all content converges on generic AI output
Hinton told Sunak to introduce UBI now; Musk pitched 'universal high income'; Lazy Owl video offers a Culture-like third way

jimmy: We are at a paradigm shift: companies now openly say AI replaces jobs, and that normalization will spread
Agentic models like Devin 'don't really work' yet — they loop and burn money; junior developers are most exposed
If everyone drafts with ChatGPT, all content converges into the same generic output
Global poverty should be fixed before anyone gets a universal high income
matt: Stealth cuts lull people into false security — named cuts at least let people act; uncertainty is the worst part
AI chips on laptops enabling offline models are potentially really positive; security concerns will limit early adoption
Most companies will chase cost savings, so governments must legislate — and it will be reactive and too late for many
Recommends funeral directing as AI-proof work; finds Lazy Owl's third scenario a genuinely hopeful vision

predictions.claim: BT will cut its workforce to roughly 75-80,000 by 2028-2030, with about 10,000 roles as direct AI replacements.
predictions.quote: They're looking to reduce that to about 75,000, 80,000 globally by 2028 to 2030. So this is pretty brutal. This is 40% of job losses that have been announced.

predictions.claim: Open 'my job was taken by AI' stories will become increasingly common as losses move from stealth to explicit.
predictions.quote: It feels to me like this is going to become more common now and we're going to start to see more of these YouTube videos, more of these stories

predictions.claim: Government legislation will arrive too late for many people and be highly reactive.
predictions.quote: I don't know how it will happen and I think I've always said I think it will be too late, too late for a lot of people. It will be very reactive.

predictions.claim: Geoffrey Hinton says the UK needs to introduce universal basic income now, without waiting.
predictions.quote: he apparently has told rishi sunak maybe this is why rishi sunak decided to step down and call an election but he's told him that the uk needs to be introducing a universal basic income now, not waiting, but doing it now.

episodes.summary: Part II sketches a 25-year socio-economic dystopia, deliberately excluding sci-fi: AI-fought wars where humans rubber-stamp machine decisions (the baseball front-office analogy), bioweapons (a 2022 study generated 40,000 chemical warfare candidates including VX in six hours), disinformation ending truth and democracy, algorithms shaping rather than reflecting preferences, mass unemployment without safety nets, US-China AI blocs, and AIs that bide their time (Holden Karnofsky). It closes with Jimmy's coined escape route: the 'AI-mish'.
keyTalkingPoints: Race-to-the-bottom dynamics (Blue Dot): misjudgment, winner-takes-all, externalities; 300:1 capability-to-alignment researchers in 2023; OpenAI dissolved its superalignment team that week
War: rumors of Lavender-style automated target selection in Gaza; the military always has the best tech version; human-in-the-loop degenerates into a Homer-Simpson button-pusher
Bio: 30,000 people could already create pathogens; AI multiplies that; benign-compound supply chains are the real control gap
Disinformation: ChatGPT Omni voice plus Sora means within 2-3 years you may trust nothing online; government plus frontier model = permanent incumbency
Algorithms now create kids' preferences from scratch — no discovery, no 'watching rubbish films to learn what a good film is'
Matt: energy is solvable via renewables; data centers' freshwater use and community displacement worry him more

jimmy: The realistic dystopia is people abusing AI, not AI acting for itself — no shred of consciousness has been seen yet
ChatGPT Omni only simulates emotion on command; disinformation will make it impossible to trust anything online within 2-3 years
Power over AI concentrated in the US big five is a pretty undemocratic application of history's biggest technology
The UK would be in a different world had it kept DeepMind instead of letting Google acquire it
matt: Dystopia avoided only two ways — a catastrophic incident or mass sentiment shift — and doing nothing is the default setting that leads there
The baseball analytics analogy shows humans will not overrule AI decisions; even figurehead humans cede real control
Government plus frontier model equals the end of democracy; scalable alignment may be impossible for superhuman models
Manipulation-worthy AI motivations are coming 'within 26 years'; water shortages from data centers matter more than energy

predictions.claim: Within two to three years we will reach a point where you cannot trust anything at all online.
predictions.quote: I'd be surprised if we don't get to a point in two to three years. Where can you trust anything at all online if you're not there already?

predictions.claim: AIs will develop their own goals and manipulate people within 26 years.
predictions.quote: You start to get their own goals and motivations and therefore manipulating and tricking people to get what? they want is the most important thing I don't know, but I think it's within 26 years.

predictions.claim: AI-mish-style communities rejecting AI will exist in the future.
predictions.quote: So I really like that term, the aimish. I wish we could patent it for the future because I think it will exist, but I wanted to finish off on on that note.

predictions.claim: Democratic backsliding would begin with absolute control of narrative and information, not literal vote-rigging.
predictions.quote: I think, initially it would be more through control of the narrative and control of information in the absolute sense, in that you would have a much more complete understanding of algorithms and how to manipulate people and how to misinform people and how to feed people whatever information you need to feed them in order to keep them on side.

episodes.summary: Part I argues an AI utopia is plausible before 2050, led by healthcare: AlphaFold 3, Insilico's FDA-approved ISM3412, DNA-personalized designer drugs, and elder-care robots arriving just as health systems collapse and populations age. They sketch UBI — or better, free energy, food and transport — squeezing inequality into a Scandinavian-style narrow band, plus democratized legal and creative services, Sora/Suno personal filmmaking, robots for dangerous jobs, AI forecasting for wicked problems, and natural-language interfaces cutting screen time.
keyTalkingPoints: ChatGPT Omni: near-real-time speech (~200ms), emotion and vision — demos included guiding a blind person through London streets and real-time translation
Tech-optimism manifesto (Andreessen) quoted at length; Matt is skeptical but concedes he is 'won over' by healthcare and equality arguments
AlphaFold 3 and Insilico's ISM3412 (FDA-approved MAT2A inhibitor) are real now; DeepMind CEO predicts AlphaFold-designed treatments on the market within two years
UBI is thinking too small — make energy, food and transport free; Altman's 'Moore's law for everything' and 'universal basic compute' get a cynical reading
Inequality will narrow like Scandinavia, but the relative-status loss for the upper-middle class is the hard part of the transition
Personal filmmaking in 5-10 years; robots for eldercare and abusive jobs; AI weather forecasting already beats traditional models

jimmy: The utopia requires governments and societies to join the debate as soon as possible
DNA-personalized designer drugs are close, and 1-to-1 fully tailored education is coming
Cannot wait to generate his own versions of Star Wars — personal AI filmmaking within 5-10 years
Cynical about Altman's motives but agrees we 'think too small' about post-work economics
matt: Healthcare is the one area where he is properly optimistic — an almost unimaginable capability in 10 years
UBI should provide the basics for a reasonable life as free goods, not just a cash payment
Democratized legal services take power away from money; narrowing inequality brings Scandinavian-style happiness
Even in utopia he spots the DNA-record dystopia; natural-language interfaces cutting screen time are a genuine positive

predictions.claim: Within two years, new drug treatments developed by AlphaFold will reach the market.
predictions.quote: It's something that the DeepMind CEO this week, when they kind of announced this, is predicting within two years that there will be new drug treatments developed by AlphaFold which will be not just created but will actually be available in the market.

predictions.claim: In 10 years, AI-driven healthcare capability will be in an almost unimaginable place.
predictions.quote: I think in 10 years time we're going to be in a, an almost unimaginable place in terms of you know what we can do with with healthcare

predictions.claim: People will be able to create their own versions of films and TV within 5-10 years.
predictions.quote: I don't have the creative ability to do it myself, but like I can see that happening in the next five to ten years.

predictions.claim: In a 25-year utopia scenario, almost no one has a traditional job and everyone is on some form of UBI.
predictions.quote: ultimately, in 25 years time, what you're saying is pretty much no one has a job. Everyone is on some form of universal basic income.

episodes.summary: The tenth-episode milestone catchup covers two months of dizzying change: Llama 3 (a 70B model ~400x smaller than GPT-4 yet beating GPT-3.5), Groq's LPU chips making inference blazingly fast, the big-three arms race, Alibaba's Qwen Audio, the gpt2-chatbot mystery model, global jailbreaks undermining safety, Suno/Stable Audio and AI slop on Spotify, China's robotics lead and Vidu versus Sora, agents arriving this autumn, physical AI devices, and 'phantom jobs' — roles advertised for months that are never filled.
keyTalkingPoints: Llama 3: 7B/70B (400B coming) runs on consumer hardware; businesses can fine-tune in-house — Jimmy considers cancelling subscriptions
Groq's language processing units infer faster than Claude Haiku, free with no signup — but knowledge cutoffs limit use
LLMs are misused as search engines; their real value is constrained drafting and coding with your own guardrails — always fact-check
EU AI Act plus rumored US rules may cap open-source model sizes — Jimmy calls it BS since closed models are globally jailbreakable
Suno v2/v3 tracks are cheesy with a telltale 'Suno style'; AI music is flooding Spotify, guided by $1,500/month scam tutorials
Agents (Google's due autumn) act in the real world; Groq+Whisper+GPT-4 mean human-indistinguishable call centers are around the corner

jimmy: Open-source models are the most exciting development — near-state-of-the-art performance on your own hardware within a year
Capping open-source model sizes is pointless when closed models can be jailbroken globally and the methods are public
Do not use LLMs as search engines — hallucination territory; use them for specific drafting tasks and fact-check everything
Real-time inference plus agents means automated call centers indistinguishable from humans are just around the corner
matt: The big three leapfrog each other endlessly; most people use LLMs as overpriced search engines and miss the point
Regulating open-source could entrench big-tech power, though policing three closed labs may be the only practical route
'Phantom jobs' — ads running five or six months, never filled — plus long-COVID workforce exits let firms cut positions quietly
The Cisco-led reskilling consortium shows industry knows regulation is coming and is positioning ahead of it

predictions.claim: Google's agent products will come out this year, probably in autumn.
predictions.quote: I think that you know the idea is that will come out this year. I think you're probably looking at autumn this year.

predictions.claim: Automated call centers indistinguishable from humans are just around the corner.
predictions.quote: means that things like automated call centers, where you can't really distinguish them from a person, are just around the corner

predictions.claim: Within a year, models comparable to GPT-3.5 will run on local machines.
predictions.quote: We're already starting to see the possibility of running something on your local machine a year down the line from chat GPT 3.5.

predictions.claim: The AI-music flood on Spotify will not last — saturation or platform crackdown will end it.
predictions.quote: I think it's something that obviously is not going to last for long, because either it will be saturated or, I would imagine, the likes of Spotify will shut it down if it starts to you know, flood, flood Spotify to the point that people the algorithm is feeding people rubbish AI tracks.

episodes.summary: Matt interviews Karen Wang, founder-CEO of Climind, a climate-focused LLM copilot built on curated datasets with RAG citations, extracting ESG data back to 2013 and answering climate-risk questions a general model would fumble. Wang argues access to information is productivity, while her biggest worries are the digital divide — climate-vulnerable regions lack frontier-tech access — and election-year chaos derailing climate policy; on jobs, she takes the optimistic line that AI creates more roles than it kills.
keyTalkingPoints: Climind's moat is a climate-specific dataset plus RAG citations; agents automate repeatable work like ESG report extraction (HKSE filings back to 2013)
Karen's thesis: access to information is productivity; users do not care if it is AI, only that the problem is solved
AI as enabler: climate-risk modeling is the real gap (short disaster histories); gains are iterative, not a silver bullet
Concerns: data-center emissions claims lack solid papers; the digital divide maps onto climate vulnerability, driving polarization
2024's elections threaten climate policy for half the globe; China skills/innovation vs US bottom-up dynamism shapes AI development
Jobs: Wang's standard view is AI will create more jobs than it kills (Jensen Huang: CS is not a great major); Matt cannot agree but hopes he is wrong

matt: Wanted a big AI climate breakthrough and is disappointed the gains are iterative rather than revolutionary
Accepts AI can crunch climate risk where human analysis is too slow, and credits Climind's citation-grounded approach
Cannot see how more jobs are created than lost this time, though he hopes Karen is right and he is wrong
Worries AI diverts capital and attention from climate; wants regulation that keeps entry channels open for small founders

No generic label is misattributed to a host in this episode.

predictions.claim: AI will create more jobs than it kills.
predictions.quote: Well, my standard view is AI will create more jobs than killing.

predictions.claim: The digital divide will compound climate vulnerability and deepen societal polarization.
predictions.quote: So I'm really worried about that because if the dynamic of society change, like how all society get lift up, how the tour the future generation can access, then it's hard to align the same level of education and the next generation. So the divide would just be bothered.

predictions.claim: Job losses from AI will not happen as fast as the scare stories claim, for structural reasons.
predictions.quote: I have started to feel like you know some of the kind of scare stories about you know you know everyone's going to lose their job Eight million jobs are going to be lost

predictions.claim: Climind is in the process of opening its platform to the general public beyond climate.
predictions.quote: But, moving forward, we are in the process of opening this to the general public, and also not just climate.

episodes.summary: Matt interviews Anders Hove of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, who argues AI's climate role is iterative — solar and battery costs fell 90-95% through manufacturing scale-up, not AI-discovered materials — and that the real barriers are policy and capital structure. Data centers (~2% of global electricity, on par with aviation) may reach 620-1050 TWh by 2026; the 85 TWh AI-server forecast for 2027 is scary but meetable by incremental renewables, and green certificates are largely accounting fiction. His fixes: mandatory disclosure and 24/7 clean-energy matching.
keyTalkingPoints: Enabler side is real but 'playing around the edges': wind/solar forecasting (DeepMind), grid flexibility, building optimization — no silver bullet

episodes.summary: The hosts test AI against the human touch in hospitality. episodes.summary: The legal episode pits augmentation against elimination: Goldman Sachs estimates 44% of legal tasks can be automated, and tools like CoCounsel and Harvey are already doing research and discovery in minutes, but hallucinated citations (the $5,000 Levidow sanction) show why humans must sign off. Guest Kelly Inga describes in-house teams building 'legal operations' functions around AI — and one employer planning to replace commercial contract lawyers with playbook software — while both hosts see AI regulation itself as the sector's growth opportunity.

episodes.summary: On executive and office work, the hosts walk through how LLMs actually work — training, hallucination, jailbreaks — before testing which roles evaporate first: receptionists, data entry, bookkeeping, basic research. Agentic tools like AutoGPT and Devin signal end-to-end automation, and Jimmy predicts 2024 brings 'drop-in replacement' AI PAs; coders keep human oversight short-term before architect-type roles remain.
